questions.q: Which compound does NOT give a coloured precipitate with Brady's reagent?
questions.explain: Brady's reagent responds only to aldehydes and ketones. In an ester the lone pair on the attached oxygen is delocalised into the C=O, so the carbonyl carbon is not electrophilic enough to react.

questions.q: The reaction of an aldehyde or ketone with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine is best described as:
options: Nucleophilic addition followed by elimination of water
questions.explain: The –NH₂ of 2,4-DNPH adds to the acid-activated carbonyl carbon to give a carbinolamine, which loses water to form the C=N of the hydrazone. It is the same condensation that forms oximes and semicarbazones.

questions.q: A compound C₈H₈O gives an orange-red precipitate with 2,4-DNPH and a yellow precipitate in the iodoform test, but does not reduce Tollens' or Fehling's reagent. The compound is:
questions.explain: A positive 2,4-DNP test shows an aldehyde or ketone, a negative Tollens'/Fehling's test rules out the aldehyde, and a positive iodoform test shows CH₃CO–. Only acetophenone, C₆H₅COCH₃, fits all three.

questions.q: Why does acetic acid give no precipitate with Brady's reagent although it contains a C=O group?
options: Its C=O group is too sterically hindered
It forms an insoluble salt with H₂SO₄
2,4-DNPH reacts only with aromatic carbonyl compounds
Resonance with the –OH lone pair makes the carbonyl carbon less electrophilic, and the acid can lose a proton to form an unreactive carboxylate
questions.explain: In acids, esters and amides the C=O is stabilised by the lone pair on the attached O or N, so the carbonyl carbon is a poor electrophile. A carboxylic acid also forms a carboxylate ion, which repels nucleophiles.
